title: API Management AI gateway
summary: An AI gateway in API Management puts token limits, token metrics, semantic caching, content safety, load balancing and a circuit breaker in front of your model deployments, so every team gets one governed endpoint.
useIf: Several apps or teams share model capacity and you need per-consumer limits, cost attribution and failover in one place.
avoidIf: One app calls one deployment and the gateway would be a new single point of failure with no policy to enforce.

explain.md: The gateway covers token limits, token metrics, semantic caching, content safety, load balancing and a circuit breaker [[r1]]. **`llm-token-limit`** limits by a `counter-key` using `tokens-per-minute`, a `token-quota` over a `token-quota-period` (`Hourly`, `Daily`, `Weekly`, `Monthly`, `Yearly`), or both. A rate breach returns 429 and a quota breach returns 403. `estimate-prompt-tokens` is required, streaming always estimates, images count up to 1,200 tokens each when estimating, and concurrent requests can briefly exceed the limit. Counters are per gateway, not aggregated across regions. V2 tiers use a token bucket and classic tiers a sliding window [[r2]].

**`llm-emit-token-metric`** sends token counts to Application Insights with up to 5 custom dimensions per policy, 100 unique values per dimension and 1,000 active time series per namespace, beyond which data is silently dropped. Streaming needs `include_usage: true` on some OpenAI models for accurate counts, and cached, reasoning and thinking categories are preview [[r3]]. The **semantic cache** uses a paired `llm-semantic-cache-lookup` and `llm-semantic-cache-store`, with `score-threshold`, `embeddings-backend-id`, `ignore-system-messages` and a `vary-by` child; Microsoft advises starting near 0.05, warns above 0.2 may mismatch, and recommends a rate limit after lookup plus content safety with Prompt Shields [[tr1]]. **Backends** carry one `circuitBreaker` rule (`failureCondition`, `tripDuration`, `acceptRetryAfter`); a tripped breaker returns 503. Pools hold up to 30 backends with round-robin, weighted or priority balancing [[r4]].

explain.title: A request path through the AI gateway
explain.alt: A client request passes semantic cache lookup, token limit and content safety, then a backend pool with a circuit breaker routes to primary or secondary. Outbound, token metrics are emitted and the answer is stored in the cache.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> SC[Cache lookup]
  SC --> TL[Token limit]
  TL --> CS[Content safety]
  CS --> P[Pool with breaker]
  P --> A[Primary backend]
  P --> B[Secondary backend]
  A --> M[Emit token metric]
  B --> M
  M --> ST[Cache store]

whereToUse: A shared platform where several teams call the same model deployments
Per-team token limits and monthly quotas for chargeback
Two or more regional deployments behind one URL with priority routing
Central token metrics in Application Insights for cost dashboards
A public FAQ where a semantic cache is acceptable

use: Many consumers share capacity and need fair shares
You want failover and load balancing without changing every client
Cost attribution by team or product is required
Content safety checks must be uniform
avoid: A single small app, where the gateway adds a hop and an outage surface
Long streaming flows that the gateway cannot pass through unbuffered
Semantic caching on permissioned or high-risk answers
flips: Stateful APIs such as Responses need session affinity, so enable it or route statefully
Multi-region traffic: counters are per gateway, so split limits per region or accept overshoot
The Foundry unified model API and AI gateway are preview: use the stable APIM policies for production

pitfalls.symptom: Dashboards miss some teams or models
pitfalls.cause: Metric dimensions exceeded 100 values or 1,000 time series and data was dropped silently [[r3]]
pitfalls.fix: Use low-cardinality dimensions such as team and model, never user id

pitfalls.symptom: Limits are exceeded briefly or overcounted
pitfalls.cause: Token counting is estimated, streaming always estimates and concurrent requests overshoot; images count up to 1,200 tokens each [[r2]]
pitfalls.fix: Leave headroom, validate against provider usage and do not treat the limit as exact billing

pitfalls.symptom: A tripped breaker looks like a model outage
pitfalls.cause: The gateway returns 503 when the circuit is open
pitfalls.fix: Tag gateway-originated errors in logs and traces and alert on open time

pitfalls.symptom: A cache hit returns another team's answer
pitfalls.cause: `vary-by` and the cache key ignored tenant, model or prompt version
pitfalls.fix: Partition by those fields or turn the cache off for that API

scenarios.title: Five teams, one deployment
scenarios.situation: Five product teams share Azure OpenAI deployments. Finance wants cost by team, and a noisy job keeps starving others.
unknowns: What dimensions are needed on metrics?
scenarios.question: What do you put in front of the deployments?

options.name: APIM with `llm-token-limit` per team and `llm-emit-token-metric` by team and model
options.why: Per-consumer rate and quota limits plus attributed metrics solve both problems in one place.
options.tradeoff: Estimated counts and brief overshoot; one more hop to operate.

options.name: A deployment per team
options.tradeoff: Fragments quota and still needs central cost reporting.

options.name: Ask the noisy team to add client-side limits
options.why: It depends on goodwill and gives no central view.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a single app with no sharing.

flips.then: Drop the gateway and use direct quota.
Set per-region limits, since counters are not aggregated.

scenarios.takeaway: A shared model needs per-consumer limits and metrics at one gate.

scenarios.title: Two regions behind one URL
scenarios.situation: A production assistant uses two Azure OpenAI resources in two regions. The primary sometimes returns 429 with a very long Retry-After.
constraints: Data may stay in either region
unknowns: Is the API stateful and needing affinity?
Is the gateway tier Consumption, which lacks circuit breakers?
scenarios.question: How do you configure it?

options.name: Priority pool with a circuit breaker that accepts Retry-After
options.why: The breaker trips on failures, honours a long Retry-After and sends traffic to the secondary, which is used only while the primary is tripped.
options.tradeoff: Breaker rules are approximate across gateway instances, and the secondary starts with a cold prompt cache.

options.name: Round-robin across both regions
options.tradeoff: Sends traffic to a failing region and splits the prompt cache all the time.

options.name: Retry the primary at the gateway until it answers
options.why: A long Retry-After means minutes or hours of wasted attempts and added load.

flips.then: Add session affinity so a conversation sticks to one backend.
Circuit breakers are unavailable, so use another tier or client-side failover.

scenarios.takeaway: Priority pools plus a breaker give automatic regional failover.

scenarios.title: A semantic cache on an HR assistant
scenarios.situation: A team proposes the gateway semantic cache for an HR assistant that answers from permissioned policy documents and employee records.
constraints: Answers depend on who is asking
unknowns: Can the cache key carry entitlement scope?
scenarios.question: Do you enable it?

options.name: No semantic cache; use prompt caching and token limits
options.why: Microsoft warns cached results can be incorrect, outdated or unsafe, and permissioned answers cannot be shared across users.
options.tradeoff: Gives up whole-call savings on repeated questions.

options.name: Enable it with a strict threshold and `vary-by` on user id
options.why: Scoping by user removes cross-user leakage.
options.tradeoff: Hit rate collapses, so the embedding cost per miss may exceed the savings.

options.name: Enable it with a loose threshold for the best hit rate
options.why: Loose matches return wrong answers and may cross users.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for public, low-risk content.

flips.if: The corpus is a public FAQ
flips.then: A strict-threshold semantic cache becomes the best option.

flips.if: Answers are identical for a whole entitlement group

scenarios.takeaway: Semantic caching is for shared, low-risk answers.

quiz.q: Clients see 503 from the gateway while the model deployment is healthy. What is the most likely cause?
options: The backend circuit breaker is tripped
quiz.explain: A tripped backend breaker returns 503 [[r4]]. A rate breach returns 429, a quota breach returns 403 [[r2]], and a cache miss falls through to the model.

quiz.q: Match each status or limit to its source.

pairs.r: Token metric namespace limit before silent drops

quiz.explain: The three codes come from three different mechanisms, which is why gateway errors should be labelled in traces [[r2]] [[r4]] [[r3]].

quiz.q: Which practices reduce the risk of a semantic cache returning the wrong user's answer?
options: Partition with `vary-by` on tenant or entitlement scope
Include model and prompt-template version in the key
Skip the cache for permissioned content
quiz.explain: Partitioning, versioned keys and skipping permissioned content reduce leakage. A looser threshold (higher in APIM) produces more wrong matches [[tr1]].

flashcards.back: 429 for the tokens-per-minute rate, 403 for the token quota. Counters are per gateway, not aggregated across regions.

flashcards.front: What happens when a backend breaker trips?
flashcards.back: The gateway returns 503. Rules are approximate across instances and unavailable in the Consumption tier. Use `acceptRetryAfter` for long Retry-After values.
5 custom dimensions per policy, 100 unique values per dimension, 1,000 active time series per namespace. Beyond that data is dropped silently.
